title: Find the real problem
outcome: Turn an ambiguous customer request into a measurable, responsible AI use case.
tasks: Map a user workflow, its friction, and the people affected.
Write a problem brief with a non-AI baseline, measurable outcome, and reason to stop the experiment.
project: Talk to a willing user about a routine task. Map the process and propose a narrow experiment with a measurable outcome.

quiz.q: A stakeholder asks for a chatbot. What comes first?
o: Understand the user, workflow, pain, and outcome.
Build a chat UI before user research.
quiz.why: Start with the user's workflow and the outcome to improve, not a presumed solution.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest prototype criterion?
o: Representative tests show faster review without more critical errors.
quiz.why: Define an observable improvement, a baseline, and a quality constraint. Specify a measurable target with the customer.

quiz.q: Required customer data is not authorized. What next?
o: Treat permissions as a constraint; change scope or stop.
Use it in a public demo.
quiz.why: Data rights constrain feasibility; prototyping does not remove this responsibility.

quiz.q: The team measures prototype value by model response speed. What is missing?
o: A user outcome and a baseline to compare against.
quiz.why: Technical latency alone does not establish that the user's task improved; choose an outcome and baseline.

quiz.q: Stakeholder opinions conflict with user observations. What is a useful next step?
o: Write down assumptions, investigate the workflow with users, and test the riskiest hypothesis.
quiz.why: Surface assumptions and collect relevant user evidence before committing to a solution.

title: Build the integration backbone
outcome: Build tested services that connect models to data and real customer workflows.
tasks: Build an API that validates inputs, handles errors explicitly, and has automated tests.
Ingest public data with a documented schema, provenance, and duplicate handling.
project: Load a public dataset into a small database and expose a paginated, tested API. Document your schema and an example error response.

quiz.q: A client sends invalid input to your API. What should happen?
o: Silently replace it with a default.
Return a documented validation error with actionable detail.
quiz.why: Explicit errors distinguish invalid requests from successful operations.

quiz.q: Why validate data with a schema at an API boundary?
o: It proves the business problem is solved.
It makes the contract explicit and catches malformed input early.
quiz.why: Validation enforces an explicit input contract; it does not replace tests or solve the business problem.

quiz.q: How do you test that an API rejects a missing required field?
o: Send an invalid request and assert its validation response.
quiz.why: Test actual invalid requests and assert the documented status and error shape.

quiz.q: An ingestion job may retry after a network failure. Which design helps avoid duplicates?
o: Assign stable record identities and make writes idempotent.
quiz.why: Idempotent operations can be retried safely without creating duplicate records.

quiz.q: A paginated API omits some records only when a client follows several pages. What should you test?
o: Pagination boundaries, ordering, and continuation behavior across multiple requests.
quiz.why: Test the actual multi-request contract and boundary cases, not just the first page.

title: Ground AI in useful knowledge
outcome: Build a retrieval-augmented assistant with inspectable evidence and visible limitations.
tasks: Build a retrieval-augmented prototype using sources you have permission to use; show your citations.
Test answerable and unanswerable questions; distinguish retrieval misses from generation errors.
project: Build a documentation assistant for a public project. Show retrieved evidence, cite the source, and flag unanswerable questions.

quiz.q: What does retrieval contribute to RAG?
o: It supplies relevant external evidence as context.
It guarantees every generated claim is true.
quiz.why: Retrieval provides context; grounding does not guarantee correctness.

quiz.q: The relevant document never appears in context. What do you investigate first?
quiz.why: Diagnose missing evidence in the retrieval pipeline separately from generation quality.

quiz.q: The source collection cannot answer a question. What should the assistant do?
o: Use any nearby passage regardless of relevance.
quiz.why: Make evidence limits visible; a nearby excerpt may not support the claim.

quiz.q: A retrieved chunk contains useful facts but no source identifier. What should you improve?
o: Preserve source metadata through retrieval so an answer can cite its evidence.
Generate a source title using the model.
quiz.why: Keep source provenance attached to retrieved passages so users can inspect actual evidence.

quiz.q: Your test answers cite the right documents but still miss the answer. What should you inspect?
o: Whether retrieved passages contain enough relevant detail and whether the question needs multiple sources.
quiz.why: Relevant source identity is not sufficient if retrieval returns incomplete evidence; inspect the content and context.

title: Turn reasoning into safe action
outcome: Give AI tools clear limits, least-privilege permissions, and human checkpoints.
tasks: Implement a narrowly scoped tool with typed inputs and independent server-side authorization.
Require human confirmation before consequential actions and test a safe failure path.
project: Build an assistant that drafts a service request using dummy data. Let a human approve submission and record each tool action.

quiz.q: A model requests a tool action. Where is authorization enforced?
o: At the server-side tool boundary using the caller's permissions.
quiz.why: A model-requested action is not authorization. The tool enforces permissions independently.

quiz.q: What is the safer default for an agent that can delete records?
o: Least privilege and explicit approval for destructive actions.
quiz.why: Constrain tool functionality and permissions; use human oversight for high-impact operations.

quiz.q: What does a structured tool schema guarantee?
o: Expected input shape, not that every call is authorized.
The model always picks the right tool.
quiz.why: Schemas describe an interface; validation, authorization, and oversight remain important.

quiz.q: A tool request contains an unexpected extra field. What is the safe handling?
o: Validate the schema and reject unsupported input before execution.
quiz.why: Validate tool input at the trusted boundary, regardless of which client proposed it.

quiz.q: An agent is asked to send an external message. What is a useful safety checkpoint?
o: Send it immediately using broad account access.
Present the proposed message and recipient for confirmation before sending.
quiz.why: Confirm important external side effects with a human, and limit the tool to necessary permissions.

title: Measure quality, not vibes
outcome: Find regressions and make responsible release decisions with representative tests.
tasks: Create a versioned test set with realistic tasks, edge cases, expected behavior, and failure modes.
Compare versions on quality, critical failures, latency, and cost; document your release decision.
project: Build an evaluation harness for your assistant. Include a failure that a polished demo would hide.

quiz.q: Which evaluation set is useful before release?
o: Representative tasks, edge cases, and failures with explicit scoring criteria.
quiz.why: Represent intended tasks and relevant risks, scored against explicit criteria.

quiz.q: You tuned on every test question. What is the concern?
o: The score may overestimate performance on new requests; reserve independent examples.
quiz.why: Keep a genuinely independent evaluation set to estimate performance beyond training or tuning examples.

quiz.q: A new version improves average quality but has a critical unsafe failure. What now?
o: Remove the example from the report.
Investigate the risk and gate the release against the documented safety criteria.
quiz.why: An aggregate improvement cannot erase a critical risk; apply the documented release gates.

quiz.q: A model upgrade changes the output format. What should you do before release?
o: Rerun the versioned evaluation, including schema and integration checks.
Assume the API contract is unchanged.
quiz.why: Evaluate behavioral and integration regressions when changing models; record the versions and outcomes.

quiz.q: A single average score hides rare but serious failures. What helps?
o: Slice results by failure type and severity and define release gates.
quiz.why: Break down results so an aggregate does not conceal failures that matter to users.

title: Ship, observe, and hand over
outcome: Deliver a maintainable service with useful observability, rollback, and a clear handoff.
tasks: Deploy a service with secret-free source, health checks, and actionable error telemetry.
Write a runbook with an owner, rollback steps, evaluation results, and customer acceptance criteria.
project: Ship your prototype to a test audience. Demonstrate failure and recovery, then hand over the operating instructions.

quiz.q: Which telemetry helps diagnose failures across an AI request with several steps?
o: Correlated traces, errors, and latency for model, retrieval, and tool steps.
quiz.why: Correlated signals help locate failures across a workflow. Avoid logging sensitive inputs unnecessarily.

quiz.q: Where should a deployed service keep API keys?
o: In protected runtime configuration, never client-delivered code.
quiz.why: Client code is public. Protect runtime credentials in an appropriate secrets store.

quiz.q: What completes an operational handoff?
o: An operator, runbook, monitoring, rollback procedure, and acceptance criteria.
quiz.why: A demo is not an operating model; include people, observability, recovery, and acceptance criteria.

quiz.q: An AI feature starts producing more errors after deployment. Which response is most operationally useful?
o: Inspect relevant error traces, alert the owner, and use the runbook to mitigate or roll back.
Wait for a customer to complain.
quiz.why: Use observable signals, a named owner, and an established mitigation or rollback procedure.

quiz.q: Who should own a deployed customer workflow after launch?
o: Nobody; deployment means the work is finished.
A named operator with a runbook, monitoring, and clear customer acceptance criteria.
quiz.why: Production delivery needs ownership, support procedures, and agreement on acceptance outcomes.
